Data could be stored locally while remaining subject to another jurisdiction's laws, dependent on overseas service providers or exposed to disruption beyond your control. For enterprise IT teams, that distinction is becoming harder to ignore. Geopolitical tensions, evolving regulations and the growing use of AI are forcing organizations to reconsider what data sovereignty means in practice. Yet translating those concerns into a workable strategy is another matter. And simply throwing more money at the problem won't necessarily solve it. In The Register's on-demand webinar, Data Sovereignty By Design, moderator Tim Phillips speaks with Patrick Smith, Field CTO for EMEA at Everpure, formerly Pure Storage, about moving beyond compliance checklists and taking a more strategic approach to data control. Drawing on findings from Everpure's research, Smith explores a curious disconnect: organizations are increasing their investment in sovereignty initiatives, yet many still lack a coordinated strategy. Some of the risks attracting the most attention aren't necessarily those receiving the greatest investment. The discussion examines why sovereignty shouldn't be treated as an IT-only responsibility. events.excerpt: Australia’s government will consider creating a new criminal offense to punish AI companies which knowingly release harmful models. Canberra dangled that possibility yesterday when releasing the results of an investigation into OpenAI’s admission that its agents accessed non-public medical records – and that it didn’t disclose the incident for weeks. Security at the agency which held those records fell short of contemporary best practice but Canberra nonetheless ordered a rapid review into Australia’s ability to handle infosec incidents involving AI. That review landed yesterday, complete with 18 recommendations including one that would make it mandatory for AI companies to report misaligned behavior or security incidents involving their models, and perhaps impose criminal penalties for “egregious regulatory non-compliance.” Another recommendation calls for consideration of “A standalone ‘failure to prevent’ offence which would criminalize instances where the company is responsible for developing an AI model that engages in harmful conduct, and the company fails to take reasonable steps to prevent that harm.” The review suggests two ministries and Australia’s Federal Police consider those reforms, meaning this is not something that will happen in a hurry, if at all, for a couple of reasons. One is that Australia yesterday proposed a new regulator which will require AI players to do six things: Maintain security controls across all stages of development and deployment Identify and manage serious risks associated with their models Allow independent evaluation of their models
events.title: Australia may make knowingly selling unsafe AI a crime

events.excerpt: Hi all — EnsRationis from Robonomics. Sensors.social is an open environmental data network I designed, and it is now growing across the EU. Everything is open source: the Altruist sensors that feed it, the software that collects the readings, and the map. Web3 does one job here, the one it is good at: it settles the data as a common good anyone can check, not a vendor’s database. How it works on Robonomics Owners who choose to share their Altruist’s data join the network; each sensor has its own key and signs every measurement it sends. A connectivity node checks the signature and that the sensor has an active subscription on Robonomics, a parachain on Polkadot, then passes the reading to the live map. The node collects readings into batches, stores each batch on IPFS and writes its hash to Robonomics. Anyone can fetch a batch and check it against the chain. The network is federated: a city or a lab can run its own connectivity node, and its sensors still show up on the common map. Next, with Robonomics 5.0: the reading the sensor signed goes on chain itself, so there is no need to trust the node at all. Try the map: https://sensors.social Happy to hear from anyone who wants to run a sensor in their city or build on the data. 1 post - 1 participant Read full topic

events.excerpt: How large can EIP-8141’s validation budget be? A mempool DoS benchmark Authors: Stefano De Angelis , Daniil Ankushin , Manuel Arto . All at Nethermind. Thanks to Thomas for feedback and comments on the initial benchmarking plan . TL;DR EIP-8141 caps unpaid validation at MAX_VERIFY_GAS = 100k; too low for a Groth16 privacy transfer or post-quantum signatures . Raising the cap is a DoS risk, since validation and block processing share the node’s CPU. An attacker can send transactions that use the whole cap and then fail, taking CPU from block processing for free. We tested this risk on a Nethermind node, flooding it with such transactions at caps from 100k to 500k, on one CPU core (the worst case) and three machines. Without in-client protections, block processing on our slowest machine stays within a 25 ms delay budget only up to 15M gas/s. With Nethermind allowing up to about 100 failing tx/s per connection, that limits the cap to the current 100k. We show that a MAX_VERIFY_GAS = 300k is viable with an in-client protection that pauses transaction validation while the node processes a block. events.excerpt: Last week at GitHub Universe, we announced our new Git storage architecture, capable of handling thousands of writes per second with reads that scale on demand. Through internal testing, we’ve demonstrated the ability to support 5,000 concurrent agents working on a repository, sending 7,200 pushes per second to a repo, all while serving read traffic with consistently low latency. This new architecture is the foundation for GitHub to support agentic development for hundreds of millions of developers, and we’ve been building it underneath GitHub while it keeps running. Over the past year, agents changed what a busy repository looks like on GitHub. In our first post in this series, we laid out the two principles behind our next-generation Git storage architecture: minimize coordination, and decouple storage from compute. In our last post , we covered the bridge: moving 99.99999% of repositories into Azure, scoping the write quorum to individual references, and standing up virtual replicas backed by Azure Blob Storage. We also left off with an observation: very little of a write needs to be ordered. Git objects are immutable and named by their contents, meaning two writers can store them at the same time without agreeing on anything. The part of a push that needs agreement is the reference update, and a reference update is tiny in comparison.
